subtopic_detail: Initiating iron removal in a C282Y homozygote with a markedly raised ferritin and no fibrosis
stem:
You are the medical registrar in a liver clinic seeing a 48-year-old man referred after abnormal blood tests taken for life insurance. He says he feels 'a bit flat and achy in the knuckles' but has no other complaints.

He drinks four standard drinks a week and takes no regular medications, vitamins or iron supplements. His father died at 61 of liver disease that was never fully investigated.

His fasting transferrin saturation is 62 per cent with a ferritin of 1150 microgram/L, repeated on a second fasting sample with the same values. HFE genotyping reports homozygosity for the C282Y variant. Alanine aminotransferase is mildly raised, C-reactive protein is within normal limits and transient elastography reports a liver stiffness of 4.8 kPa. Fasting glucose and an echocardiogram are both normal.

data_table.Iron studies: Fasting transferrin saturation 62 per cent (15-45), ferritin 1150 microgram/L (30-300), confirmed on a repeat fasting sample
data_table.Genetics: HFE genotype homozygous for the C282Y variant
data_table.Liver assessment: Alanine aminotransferase 68 U/L (less than 45), C-reactive protein within normal limits, transient elastography 4.8 kPa
data_table.Other results: Fasting glucose and echocardiogram within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Start oral deferasirox and repeat the ferritin measurement in three months
options.rationale: Chelation is reserved for iron overload in people who cannot be venesected, principally those with transfusion dependent anaemias, and it carries renal, hepatic and gastrointestinal toxicity. Venesection is cheaper, faster and better tolerated in a man with normal haemoglobin. (Source: GESA: Haemochromatosis)

options.text: Start weekly venesection aiming for a ferritin of 50 to 100 microgram/L
options.rationale: C282Y homozygosity with a fasting transferrin saturation above 45 per cent and a ferritin above the reference range, in the absence of inflammation or alcohol excess, establishes iron overload that warrants treatment. Weekly removal of 450 to 500 mL continues until the ferritin reaches 50 to 100 microgram/L, after which maintenance venesection every 3 to 4 months keeps it in that range. (Source: GESA: Haemochromatosis)

options.text: Advise dietary iron restriction and repeat the ferritin in twelve months
options.rationale: Dietary measures cannot remove the iron already deposited and have only a marginal effect on ongoing absorption, so they are an adjunct rather than a treatment. Avoiding iron and vitamin C supplements and uncooked shellfish is sensible advice alongside venesection. (Source: GESA: Haemochromatosis)

options.text: Arrange liver biopsy before any decision about starting iron removal
options.rationale: Biopsy is used to assess fibrosis when the ferritin exceeds 1000 microgram/L with raised transaminases and non-invasive assessment is equivocal, and here transient elastography at 4.8 kPa already indicates the absence of significant fibrosis. Venesection is started regardless of the fibrosis stage. (Source: GESA: Haemochromatosis)

options.text: Repeat the iron studies fasting in three months before starting treatment
options.rationale: Repeat fasting testing is the right step when a single raised ferritin could reflect inflammation, alcohol or metabolic syndrome, and that has already been done with concordant results and a normal C-reactive protein. Further delay allows continued deposition in liver, pancreas, heart and joints. (Source: GESA: Haemochromatosis)

explanation.summary: Hereditary haemochromatosis in people of northern European ancestry is overwhelmingly caused by homozygosity for the C282Y variant in HFE, which reduces hepcidin production and allows unregulated intestinal iron absorption. Penetrance is incomplete, so many homozygotes never develop clinical disease, and the decision to treat rests on the iron indices rather than on the genotype alone. Transferrin saturation rises first and is the more specific marker, while ferritin is an acute phase reactant that is also raised by alcohol, inflammation and metabolic dysfunction, which is why both are measured fasting and interpreted together with a C-reactive protein. Venesection is remarkably effective and, when started before cirrhosis develops, restores a normal life expectancy; established cirrhosis does not reverse and carries an ongoing hepatocellular carcinoma risk that requires six monthly surveillance. First-degree relatives are offered genetic and biochemical screening, since identifying them before organ damage occurs is the main benefit of making the diagnosis.
key_points: Transferrin saturation rises before ferritin and is the more specific marker of iron loading
Treat on the basis of the iron indices, not on the genotype alone, since penetrance is incomplete
Weekly venesection until ferritin reaches 50 to 100 microgram/L, then maintenance every 3 to 4 months
Life expectancy is normal if treatment starts before cirrhosis develops
Screen first-degree relatives genetically and biochemically
explanation.pearls: Arthropathy of the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints is the one manifestation that does not improve with venesection and can progress despite normal iron indices, so its presence should not be used to judge the adequacy of treatment.

subtopic_detail: Action on a first isolation of Pseudomonas aeruginosa in stable bronchiectasis
stem:
You are the medical registrar in a respiratory clinic seeing a 56-year-old woman with bronchiectasis confirmed on high resolution computed tomography five years ago following childhood pertussis. She attends for a routine review and says she is 'about the same as always'.

She produces around 20 mL of mucoid sputum daily, has had no increase in volume or change in colour, no fever and no new breathlessness, and has not had an exacerbation for eight months. She performs airway clearance twice daily and her forced expiratory volume in one second is unchanged from six months ago at 72 per cent predicted.

Her previous sputum cultures over five years have consistently grown Haemophilus influenzae. The routine sputum sample collected at her last visit has grown Pseudomonas aeruginosa for the first time, sensitive to ciprofloxacin and to tobramycin.

data_table.Symptoms: 20 mL mucoid sputum daily, unchanged; no fever, no new breathlessness, no exacerbation for eight months
data_table.Lung function: Forced expiratory volume in one second 72 per cent predicted, unchanged from six months ago
data_table.Microbiology: First isolation of Pseudomonas aeruginosa, sensitive to ciprofloxacin and tobramycin; all previous cultures grew Haemophilus influenzae

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Attempt eradication with oral ciprofloxacin and nebulised tobramycin
options.rationale: A first isolation of Pseudomonas aeruginosa in bronchiectasis is treated with an eradication attempt even when the patient is clinically stable, because chronic infection is independently associated with more exacerbations, faster lung function decline and higher mortality. The usual Australian regimen combines two weeks of oral ciprofloxacin with a course of nebulised tobramycin, with repeat cultures to confirm clearance. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Bronchiectasis Toolbox)

options.text: Start long term azithromycin three times weekly and repeat the sputum culture
options.rationale: Long term macrolide therapy reduces exacerbation frequency in patients having three or more exacerbations a year, and she has had none for eight months. Starting a macrolide also requires excluding non-tuberculous mycobacterial infection first, or resistance may be induced. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Bronchiectasis Toolbox)

options.text: Observe and repeat the sputum culture in three months if she remains well
options.rationale: Waiting allows the organism to establish a biofilm, after which eradication becomes much less likely and treatment shifts to lifelong suppression. Observation is appropriate for organisms of low pathogenic significance in bronchiectasis, which Pseudomonas aeruginosa is not. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Bronchiectasis Toolbox)

options.text: Start inhaled corticosteroid with a long acting beta agonist and review her
options.rationale: Inhaled corticosteroids are not routinely indicated in bronchiectasis without coexisting asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and they increase the risk of respiratory infection including Pseudomonas colonisation. They do nothing to clear an established isolate. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Bronchiectasis Toolbox)

options.text: Refer for surgical resection of the most affected bronchiectatic segment
options.rationale: Resection is considered for localised disease causing recurrent severe exacerbations or massive haemoptysis that has failed medical management. Her disease is stable and this would not address an organism present throughout the airway. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Bronchiectasis Toolbox)

explanation.summary: Bronchiectasis management rests on four pillars: airway clearance and exercise, treatment of exacerbations, long term suppression where exacerbations are frequent, and identification and treatment of the underlying cause. Pseudomonas aeruginosa occupies a special position because chronic infection with it marks a distinct trajectory, with more frequent exacerbations, greater sputum volume, accelerated decline in forced expiratory volume and increased mortality independent of other severity markers. For that reason a first isolation triggers an eradication attempt even in a clinically stable patient, borrowing the strategy established in cystic fibrosis, typically oral ciprofloxacin combined with an inhaled antipseudomonal agent. Once biofilm formation has occurred the organism is rarely cleared and management shifts to long term suppression with nebulised antibiotics. Investigation for a treatable underlying cause continues alongside, including immunoglobulins, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis serology, cystic fibrosis testing where appropriate, and consideration of primary ciliary dyskinesia.
key_points: Chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection independently predicts decline and mortality
A first isolation warrants an eradication attempt even when the patient is stable
Typical regimen is oral ciprofloxacin plus a nebulised antipseudomonal agent with repeat cultures
Long term macrolides are for three or more exacerbations a year, after excluding mycobacteria
Inhaled corticosteroids are not routine in bronchiectasis without asthma or airflow obstruction
explanation.pearls: Exclude non-tuberculous mycobacterial infection with three sputum cultures before starting long term azithromycin in bronchiectasis: macrolide monotherapy against an unrecognised Mycobacterium avium complex infection induces resistance and removes the most effective drug from any future regimen.

subtopic_detail: Withdrawing a long standing nightly benzodiazepine after recurrent falls in an older woman
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing an 82-year-old woman in a falls clinic. She has fallen twice in three months, once in the hallway on the way to the toilet at 2 am and once getting out of bed in the morning, and says she 'just went down' both times with no warning and no chest pain or palpitations.

She lives alone in a single storey unit and manages her own shopping. She has taken temazepam 20 mg every night for eleven years, originally started after her husband died, and says she 'could not possibly sleep without it'. She also takes sertraline 50 mg daily and perindopril.

Lying and standing blood pressures show no postural drop. Gait is slow but steady with a normal timed up and go test, visual acuity is corrected to 6/9 bilaterally and cognition is intact. Her estimated glomerular filtration rate is 48 mL/min/1.73m2. An electrocardiogram and a vitamin D level are both within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, blood pressure 132/76 mmHg lying with no postural drop, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6°C
data_table.Medications: Temazepam 20 mg nightly for eleven years, sertraline 50 mg daily, perindopril
data_table.Falls assessment: Timed up and go test within normal limits, gait slow but steady, corrected visual acuity 6/9 bilaterally, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Estimated glomerular filtration rate 48 mL/min/1.73m2, electrocardiogram and vitamin D within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Stop the temazepam tonight and start modified release melatonin instead
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation after eleven years of continuous use risks rebound insomnia, anxiety, and in some cases seizures and delirium, and it almost always drives the patient to resume the drug. Melatonin is a reasonable adjunct during a taper but does not make abrupt withdrawal safe. (Source: NPS MedicineWise: Benzodiazepine deprescribing)

options.text: Continue the temazepam and refer her to a falls prevention programme only
options.rationale: Exercise based falls prevention reduces falls and should be arranged, but leaving the single most modifiable pharmacological risk factor in place treats around the problem. Benzodiazepine use roughly doubles the risk of falls and hip fracture in older people. (Source: NPS MedicineWise: Benzodiazepine deprescribing)

options.text: Reduce the temazepam by about a quarter every two to four weeks with support
options.rationale: Benzodiazepine withdrawal in long term users is achieved by gradual dose reduction of roughly 10 to 25 per cent every 2 to 4 weeks, slowing further near the end where withdrawal symptoms are most pronounced. Pairing the taper with education and behavioural strategies for insomnia substantially increases the proportion who stop successfully. (Source: NPS MedicineWise: Benzodiazepine deprescribing)

options.text: Switch her to nightly zopiclone at an equivalent dose and review in a month
options.rationale: The so-called Z drugs carry the same falls, fracture and cognitive risks as benzodiazepines in older people and are not a safer substitute. Substitution also resets the dependence rather than reducing total sedative exposure. (Source: NPS MedicineWise: Benzodiazepine deprescribing)

options.text: Switch her to nightly diazepam at an equivalent dose and review in a month
options.rationale: Conversion to a long acting agent is a recognised technique that smooths withdrawal for short acting drugs such as alprazolam, but temazepam has an intermediate half-life and tapers adequately in its own right. Diazepam accumulates markedly in older people with reduced renal and hepatic clearance, and the active metabolite prolongs the sedative and falls risk. (Source: NPS MedicineWise: Benzodiazepine deprescribing)

explanation.summary: Falls in older people are multifactorial, and a structured assessment covers gait and balance, vision, postural blood pressure, cognition, continence, footwear, home hazards and medications. Benzodiazepines, Z drugs, antipsychotics, anticholinergics, opioids and antidepressants are the principal culprit medicine classes, and benzodiazepines approximately double the risk of falls and hip fracture in this age group. Long term use is rarely justified for insomnia because tolerance to the hypnotic effect develops within weeks while the daytime psychomotor and cognitive impairment persists. Deprescribing succeeds far more often when the patient understands the rationale, when reduction is gradual rather than abrupt, and when non-pharmacological treatment for insomnia is offered in parallel. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia outperforms hypnotics for chronic insomnia at every age and its benefit persists after treatment ends.
key_points: Benzodiazepines roughly double the risk of falls and hip fracture in older people
Reduce by about 10 to 25 per cent every 2 to 4 weeks, slowing near the end of the taper
Never stop abruptly after long term use because of rebound, seizure and delirium risk
Z drugs carry the same risks and are not a safer substitute
Offer cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia alongside the taper
explanation.pearls: Switching to diazepam before tapering is genuinely useful for short half-life agents like alprazolam and oxazepam, where interdose withdrawal drives the difficulty, but it is counterproductive in frail older people because the active metabolite desmethyldiazepam has a half-life that can exceed 100 hours.

subtopic_detail: Advising a man in his mid fifties whose father was diagnosed with prostate cancer after age sixty
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 55-year-old man for a routine review of his blood pressure. Towards the end of the consultation he says a colleague has told him to 'get the prostate test' and asks whether he should have it.

His father was diagnosed with prostate cancer at the age of 62 and is alive and well eight years after treatment. He has no brothers. No other family members have had prostate, breast or ovarian cancer.

He passes urine twice a night, which he says has been the same for years, with a normal stream and no haematuria and no bone pain. Digital rectal examination has never been performed. He is otherwise well, works full time, and tells you he would want treatment if something were found.

data_table.Family history: Father diagnosed with prostate cancer at age 62 and well eight years after treatment; no brothers; no family history of breast or ovarian cancer
data_table.Urinary symptoms: Nocturia twice nightly, unchanged for years, normal stream, no haematuria
data_table.Other: No bone pain, works full time, would accept treatment if a cancer were found

options.text: Arrange a prostate specific antigen test and a digital rectal examination today
options.rationale: Digital rectal examination adds negligible diagnostic value to prostate specific antigen testing in asymptomatic men in primary care and is no longer recommended as part of screening. Ordering the antigen test without first discussing the benefits and harms also bypasses the consent process the guideline requires. (Source: PCFA and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines)
source_refs: PCFA and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines

options.text: Advise against testing and review him again when he turns sixty years old
options.rationale: Blanket advice against testing is not what Australian guidance recommends for a man aged 50 to 69 who asks about it, and deferring to 60 would forfeit a decade of the age band in which testing offers most benefit. Testing is not recommended in men whose life expectancy is under 7 years, which does not apply here. (Source: PCFA and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines)
source_refs: PCFA and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines

options.text: Refer him directly to urology for multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging
options.rationale: Multiparametric imaging is used after a raised prostate specific antigen to decide whether and where to biopsy, not as a first-line screening test in an asymptomatic man. Using it up front would generate incidental findings without an antigen result to interpret them against. (Source: PCFA and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines)
source_refs: PCFA and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines

options.text: Arrange a prostate specific antigen test yearly from now until age seventy
options.rationale: Annual testing increases the detection of indolent disease and the associated overtreatment without a corresponding mortality benefit, which is why the recommended interval is every 2 years. The age band is also to 69 rather than to 70. (Source: PCFA and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines)
source_refs: PCFA and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines

options.text: Discuss the benefits and harms and recommend two yearly testing to age 69
options.rationale: Australian guidance is that men aged 50 to 69 who decide to be tested after being informed of the benefits and harms should be offered prostate specific antigen testing every 2 years, and a father diagnosed after 60 confers a modestly increased risk that does not change the starting age. The discussion covers the reduction in prostate cancer mortality set against overdiagnosis, biopsy complications, and the incontinence and erectile dysfunction that follow treatment of disease that would never have caused harm. (Source: PCFA and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines)
source_refs: PCFA and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines

explanation.summary: Prostate specific antigen testing is offered rather than recommended universally, because the mortality benefit is real but modest while overdiagnosis is substantial, and Australian guidance therefore builds the decision around an informed discussion. For men at average risk the recommendation is two yearly testing between 50 and 69 years for those who choose to be tested, with no testing where life expectancy is less than about 7 years. Family history modifies the starting age rather than the interval: a first-degree relative diagnosed under 60, or two or more affected relatives, moves the start to 45, and a very strong family history or a known BRCA2 mutation moves it to 40. A father diagnosed at 62 raises the relative risk modestly and does not by itself bring the start forward. Digital rectal examination is no longer recommended as an addition to antigen testing in asymptomatic men in general practice, and a raised result is now usually followed by multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging before any decision about biopsy.
key_points: Offer two yearly testing between 50 and 69 after discussing benefits and harms
A first-degree relative diagnosed under 60 brings the starting age forward to 45
A relative diagnosed after 60 raises risk modestly without changing the starting age
Digital rectal examination adds little in asymptomatic men and is no longer recommended
Do not test where life expectancy is less than about 7 years
explanation.pearls: A prostate specific antigen above the age specific 95th centile, which is 3.0 microgram/L for men in their fifties, prompts a repeat within 1 to 3 months before referral, because transient rises from ejaculation, cycling, prostatitis or instrumentation are common and a single raised value is not an indication for biopsy.

sources.label: PCFA and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines
RACGP: Guidelines for preventive activities in general practice
BMJ Best Practice: Prostate cancer screening

subtopic_detail: Rash with fever, eosinophilia and hepatitis six weeks after starting a urate lowering drug
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 64-year-old man from the emergency department with a rash and fever. He says it started around his neck nine days ago and 'has taken over everywhere', and that his face feels tight and swollen.

He started allopurinol 300 mg daily six weeks ago for recurrent gout. He takes perindopril and has taken no new antibiotics, herbal preparations or over the counter medicines.

On examination there is a confluent morbilliform eruption covering the trunk, both arms and both legs with marked periorbital and facial oedema. The lips, conjunctivae and oral mucosa are unaffected, there is no skin detachment and Nikolsky sign is negative. There is tender cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy. Investigations are shown.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108/min, blood pressure 128/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 38.9°C
data_table.Skin: Confluent morbilliform eruption over trunk and all four limbs with facial and periorbital oedema; mucosae spared; no skin detachment; Nikolsky sign negative
data_table.Investigations: Eosinophils 2.4 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5), white cell count 16.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0) with atypical lymphocytes, alanine aminotransferase 320 U/L (less than 45), creatinine 142 micromol/L (60-110) rising from 88 micromol/L
data_table.Medications: Allopurinol 300 mg daily started six weeks ago; perindopril long term

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Stop the allopurinol and start topical corticosteroid with an oral antihistamine
options.rationale: Topical treatment and antihistamines are appropriate for a simple morbilliform drug eruption, which is confined to the skin without fever, facial oedema, eosinophilia or organ involvement. Restricting treatment to the skin here leaves a hepatitis and an acute kidney injury untreated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Continue the allopurinol and start oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg each morning
options.rationale: Immediate and permanent withdrawal of the culprit drug is the single most important intervention and determines outcome, so corticosteroid without withdrawal is inadequate. Allopurinol also has a long acting metabolite, oxipurinol, so the reaction can continue to evolve for weeks after cessation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Stop the allopurinol and transfer him to a burns unit for specialist skin care
options.rationale: Burns unit transfer is the pathway for Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, which present with mucosal erosions, a positive Nikolsky sign and epidermal detachment. His mucosae are spared with no detachment, and the eosinophilia and hepatitis point to a different reaction pattern. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Stop the allopurinol and start oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg each morning
options.rationale: Rash with fever, facial oedema, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia above 1.5 x10^9/L and hepatic and renal involvement 2 to 8 weeks after starting a drug is a drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms, and allopurinol is among the commonest causes. The drug is withdrawn permanently and systemic corticosteroid at 0.5 to 1 mg/kg is given for organ involvement, weaned slowly over 8 to 12 weeks because rapid reduction provokes relapse. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Stop the allopurinol and start intravenous immunoglobulin over five days
options.rationale: Immunoglobulin is used in severe toxic epidermal necrolysis and in some refractory presentations, and it is not first-line treatment for this reaction pattern. Corticosteroid remains the mainstay where there is organ involvement. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

explanation.summary: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms is a severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction distinguished from other drug eruptions by its long latency of 2 to 8 weeks, its systemic features and its tendency to persist and relapse after the drug is stopped. The characteristic combination is fever, an extensive morbilliform or oedematous eruption, facial oedema, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia or atypical lymphocytosis, and involvement of at least one internal organ, most often the liver. Allopurinol, aromatic anticonvulsants such as carbamazepine, phenytoin and lamotrigine, sulfonamides, vancomycin and minocycline account for the majority of cases. Reactivation of human herpesvirus 6 and other herpesviruses occurs during the illness and contributes to the relapsing course and to the late complications, which include thyroiditis and type 1 diabetes appearing months afterwards. Mortality is around 5 to 10 per cent, mostly from fulminant hepatitis, and long term follow-up with thyroid and glucose monitoring is recommended.
key_points: Latency is 2 to 8 weeks, far longer than a simple morbilliform eruption
Look for fever, facial oedema, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia and organ involvement
Allopurinol and the aromatic anticonvulsants are the commonest culprits
Withdraw the drug permanently and treat organ involvement with systemic corticosteroid
Wean corticosteroid over 8 to 12 weeks and monitor thyroid function for months afterwards
explanation.pearls: Test for HLA-B*58:01 before starting allopurinol in people of Han Chinese, Thai or Korean ancestry: carriage confers a markedly increased risk of severe cutaneous adverse reaction and the alternative urate lowering agent is febuxostat.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms
